title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated license plate reader that was acted on as though it were a confirmed identification. The system misread a single character, produced a match to a stolen vehicle, and the match was wrong. The failure is not that the reader erred, it is that its output was treated as a fact sufficient to justify drawing a weapon on a motorist.

The failure sits at the handoff between the alert and the enforcement action, the point where a machine-generated match becomes a physical stop. Flock's own stated position is that alerts should be independently verified before enforcement, and the account describes no such verification between the misread and the detention. The sheriff's office attributes the malfunction to an illegal tinted plate cover, which places the input outside the conditions the reader handles reliably.

Catching it would have required a human comparing the plate on the vehicle to the plate in the alert before the stop, which is the check the vendor says should occur. What is not established is the cause: the tinted cover is the sheriff's account rather than an independent finding, and the same office's conclusion that the deputy acted reasonably is an internal review, not an adjudication. A single outlet's report is not proof of what the reader did or why.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, a motorist in York County, South Carolina, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety license plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and found the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
